newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Better times seen for Pakistan brokerage firms.
newsitem.headline: Better times seen for Pakistan brokerage firms.

text.p: Brokerage houses in Pakistan have suffered along with the battered national economy, but analysts said on Monday that new government incentives offered a possibility of better performances in 1997.

"Some brokerage houses are playing cautiously as they think the incentives announced by the caretaker government are temporary and they might be changed by the government to be inducted after the February 3 polls," said dealer Ali Raza of Kausar Abbas Bhayani Securities Ltd.

The caretaker government was installed by President Farooq Leghari after the November 5 dismissal of Benazir Bhutto's government on disputed charges of corruption and misrule. It has pledged to hold national and provincial elections on February 3.

"But overall prospects are good and market men are expecting a rise in the prices of stocks and the Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) index," Raza said. "We hope the brokerage houses' performance will be much better in 1997 than 1996."

The government unveiled a stock market package last week that included removing 10 percent withholding tax on bonus shares, exempting insurance companies from capital gains tax and allowing the repurchase of up to 10 percent of treasury stocks.
The government has also offered incentives to the textile sector, the backbone of Pakistani industry.
A research report by Kausar Abbas Bhayani Securities Ltd said brokerage houses had mushroomed in the past six years, matching the growth in Pakistan's capital market.
The number of listed companies rose to 782 in 1996 from 487 in 1990 and market capitalisation jumped to more than 500 billion rupees ($12.43 billion) from 61.8 billion, it said.
But relatively few brokerages had sought listing at the KSE. "The main deterrent...could be the prevailing market conditions with a sort of passive response to new issues," the report said.
Only 24 of the KSE's 200 members had taken corporate membership and only seven were publicly listed. Four of these declared a loss for 1996 and three had a book value below par.

The main reason was the market's persistent decline since the index hit its record high of 2,661 points in March 1994, the report said. This had limited institutional and foreign interest, which in any case was concentrated on five stocks that account for about 80 percent of trading volume.

"The main reasons cited for poor market performance are high fiscal deficits, a widening trade gap, devaluation, increased government borrowing from domestic and international market, inflation, the downgrading of the country's credit rating and the law and order situation," the report said.
In this macro environment, the market traded in a narrow range, limiting brokerage income except for some snap news, which generated high volume for a very limited period, it said.

"The gain on sale of investments was not there, instead there was a big burden for making the provision for diminution in the value of investments, to eat into whatever profits were earned from equity brokerage and the results exhibited that."

"The main activity of brokerage houses, of course, is equity brokerage, but due to high exposure to investment portfolio, the hard-earned brokerage income was somewhat overshadowed by magnified capital gains or losses," the report said.
